clinicalPearls: Defined on high-resolution manometry (Chicago Classification) by at least two swallows with markedly elevated distal contractile integral above the hypercontractile threshold, with preserved peristaltic sequence.

The exaggerated contractions may involve repetitive or multi-peaked waves and can include vigorous contraction of the lower oesophageal sphincter, distinguishing it from diffuse spasm where contractions are premature rather than merely vigorous.
Chest pain and dysphagia are the dominant complaints; a proportion of patients are minimally symptomatic and the manometric finding is incidental.
Always exclude obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction, as outflow resistance (including early achalasia or a tight fundoplication) can provoke a compensatory hypercontractile pattern.
Coexisting gastro-oesophageal reflux and oesophageal hypersensitivity are common and should be actively assessed and treated.
Smooth-muscle relaxants and neuromodulators (tricyclics, other visceral analgesics) form first-line therapy; peppermint oil may reduce contractile vigour.
Endoscopic botulinum toxin injection can give temporary relief, and peroral endoscopic myotomy is reserved for refractory, clearly symptom-correlated disease.
The diagnosis carries prognostic uncertainty because some patients progress to spastic achalasia, so follow-up manometry may be warranted if symptoms evolve.
reference.pathophysiology: Jackhammer oesophagus is a hypercontractile disorder of the oesophageal smooth-muscle segment defined by excessively vigorous peristaltic contractions, quantified by an abnormally high distal contractile integral. The peristaltic sequence remains intact, distinguishing it from the premature contractions of distal spasm. The underlying mechanism is thought to involve an imbalance favouring excitatory cholinergic drive over inhibitory nitrergic input to the oesophageal musculature, sometimes compounded by asynchronous or prolonged contraction of the longitudinal and circular muscle layers and hypertrophy of the muscularis. In a subset, hypercontractility is a secondary or compensatory response to distal outflow obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction. Oesophageal hypersensitivity contributes substantially to symptom generation, which explains the frequent dissociation between manometric severity and clinical severity.
additionalDifferentials: functional chest pain and oesophageal hypersensitivity
additionalInvestigations: high-resolution oesophageal manometry with distal contractile integral quantification
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude mucosal, structural and obstructing lesions
timed barium oesophagram to assess emptying and outflow
functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) to evaluate oesophagogastric junction distensibility
provocative testing (multiple rapid swallows, solid test meal) during manometry
redFlags: progressive dysphagia or weight loss suggesting evolving achalasia or mechanical obstruction
chest pain requiring urgent exclusion of acute coronary syndrome
food bolus impaction or inability to manage secretions
manometric evidence of impaired oesophagogastric junction relaxation indicating an obstructive process
rapid symptom progression in an older patient raising concern for malignant pseudo-obstruction
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are variable and often benign, with many patients stable or improving on medical therapy and neuromodulation; symptom severity correlates poorly with manometric findings. A minority progress to spastic achalasia or have refractory symptoms, and response to myotomy is less predictable than in classic achalasia.
pitfalls: Diagnosing jackhammer oesophagus without excluding oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction that can secondarily drive hypercontractility.
Assuming that severe manometric findings mandate invasive therapy in a patient who is minimally symptomatic.
Overlooking coexistent reflux and hypersensitivity as treatable contributors to chest pain.
Failing to repeat manometry when symptoms evolve, thereby missing progression to spastic achalasia.
Attributing chest pain to the manometric abnormality before cardiac disease has been excluded.

ACG Clinical Guideline on oesophageal motility disorders
management: Smooth-muscle relaxants such as calcium-channel blockers and nitrates, with peppermint oil, to reduce contractile vigour
Neuromodulators such as tricyclic antidepressants for pain and oesophageal hypersensitivity
Assess for and treat coexisting gastro-oesophageal reflux with proton-pump inhibitors
Exclude oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction, including early achalasia or a tight fundoplication, before attributing symptoms to primary hypercontractility
Peroral endoscopic myotomy or botulinum toxin injection for selected refractory symptomatic patients
Reassurance and conservative management given the frequently benign course and poor correlation between symptoms and manometric findings
